title: The decontamination room: dirty to clean
blurb: The one-way workflow, how the room is laid out, and what to do when clean and dirty get mixed up.
question: You are covering the decontamination room on a busy morning. The dirty bench is full, so a colleague puts a tray of used instruments on the packing bench, right next to some freshly sterilised pouches. What should you do, and why does the layout of the room matter so much?

teach.body: Decontamination makes a used instrument safe to use on the next patient. HTM 01-05 says it must follow a dirty-to-clean workflow: instruments move one way through each stage, so that at no point is a clean instrument recontaminated by a surface or item from an earlier, dirtier stage. Everything about the room, from where the sinks sit to which way the air flows, is designed to protect that one-way journey.

teach.caption: After use the instrument is dirty again and the loop restarts. Skip or rush any stage and the instruments that come out are not safe.

teach.h: Dirty to clean along the bench

steps.label: Receive
steps.sub: Dirty set-down bench, used for nothing else

steps.label: Sterilise
steps.sub: Sited away from the other activities

teach.caption: The receiving area sits next to the wash stage and furthest from clean storage. Where possible, air moves the opposite way: from clean to dirty.

teach.body: Used instruments go to the decontamination area as soon as possible so debris doesn't dry on. They travel in a container that is rigid, leak-proof, easy to clean and closes securely. Containers for dirty and for sterilised instruments are clearly marked and never swapped. Dirty items never travel through the clean area, and clean and dirty loads never share a trolley. The room also holds the right waste containers, so waste is segregated where it is made.

teach.h: Essential quality requirements and best practice
teach.body: HTM 01-05 sets two levels. Essential quality requirements are the minimum for every practice: decontamination may happen in, or next to, a surgery, but separated from clinical work by space or by time, as far from the chair as practical. Manual washing, an uncovered ultrasonic or opening a machine must not happen while a patient is present. Best practice means a separate decontamination room (two rooms, dirty and clean, is preferred), a validated washer-disinfector and better storage. Practices at the essential level need a plan to progress.

teach.caption: Each unsafe habit is a recontamination risk for instruments that have already been processed.

teach.h: Which zone does it belong in?
teach.note: Clear 'dirty' and 'clean' signs help new and agency staff follow the flow. Clean packs are never stored above or under the dirty sink, where splashes reach them.

teach.h: When clean and dirty get mixed up
items: Stop. Don't carry on packing or unloading.
Treat anything whose status is uncertain as dirty and move it to the dirty zone.
Remove your gloves and perform hand hygiene.
Clean and disinfect the contaminated clean surface before using it again.
Reprocess any pack that touched dirty items or whose status you can't be sure of.
Tell the decontamination lead so the cause can be fixed.

teach.text: Gloves cross zones too. The heavy-duty gloves you cleaned instruments in must come off, followed by hand hygiene, before you touch clean packs, pens or paperwork. And the decontamination sinks are never used for hand washing: use the separate wash-hand basin.

items: One-way flow: receive dirty, clean, inspect, pack, sterilise, store.
Receiving area next to the wash stage, furthest from clean storage; sterile packs move last.
Dirty and clean containers, trolleys and routes are never shared.
Essential quality: designated area separated by space or time. Best practice: separate room and washer-disinfector.
Mixed up? Stop, separate, clean the surface, reprocess anything uncertain.

summary: You can now describe the decontamination cycle and the dirty-to-clean workflow, explain how the room is laid out and why, tell essential quality requirements from best practice, and act correctly when clean and dirty items are mixed up.

A.q: The dirty bench is full, so a colleague puts a tray of used instruments on the clean packing bench beside sterilised pouches. What is the best action?
options: Leave it there until the pouches are put away in storage
Cover the tray with a paper towel
Move it to the dirty zone and clean the bench
Wipe the pouches with alcohol later on
A.why: Dirty items must go straight back to the dirty zone, and the contaminated clean surface must be decontaminated before it is used again.

whyNot.0: Leaving it there keeps the clean zone contaminated and puts the pouches at risk.
whyNot.1: A paper towel doesn't stop contamination of the bench or nearby packs.
whyNot.3: Wiping the pouches later doesn't fix the contaminated bench, and any pack that touched dirty items should be reprocessed.

A.q: A practice is planning a new decontamination room. Which item should be positioned nearest the washing stage?
options: The used-instrument receiving area
The clean storage cupboards
The pouch sealing machine
The sterilised-pack cooling bench
A.why: Dirty instruments arrive at the receiving area, which sits beside the wash stage at the dirty end, furthest from clean storage.

whyNot.1: Clean storage belongs at the far, clean end of the room.
whyNot.2: Packing happens on the clean side after inspection.
whyNot.3: Sterilised packs cool on the clean side, well away from washing.

A.q: Under HTM 01-05, which feature is part of best practice rather than the essential quality requirements?
options: A one-way dirty-to-clean workflow
Audit of decontamination practice every six months
A separate wash-hand basin for staff
A validated washer-disinfector in its own room
A.why: Best practice includes a separate decontamination room and a validated washer-disinfector. The other three are expected of every practice.

whyNot.0: A dirty-to-clean workflow is required at every level.
whyNot.1: Six-monthly audit is a minimum requirement for all practices.
whyNot.2: A dedicated wash-hand basin is an essential requirement.

B.q: To save time, a nurse carries a tray of used instruments through the clean storage area to reach the sink. What is the main problem?
options: It breaks the one-way workflow
It makes the tray heavier to carry
It delays the sterilisation cycle
It uses the wrong type of gloves
B.why: Dirty items must never travel through clean areas. A designated dirty route protects processed instruments from recontamination.

whyNot.1: Weight isn't the issue; contamination of the clean area is.
whyNot.2: Timing isn't the problem; the route is.
whyNot.3: Glove type isn't the main concern here; carrying dirty items through a clean zone is.

B.q: A practice meets the essential quality requirements and reprocesses instruments in the surgery. Which activity must NOT happen while a patient is present?
options: Writing up the sterilizer logbook
Manual washing of used instruments
Placing a sterilised pouch in a drawer
Restocking single-use saliva ejectors
B.why: HTM 01-05 says activities that create splashes or aerosols, such as manual washing, an uncovered ultrasonic or opening decontamination equipment, must not take place while the patient is present.

whyNot.0: Writing in the logbook creates no splash or aerosol risk.
whyNot.2: Storing a sealed pouch doesn't create splashes or aerosols.
whyNot.3: Restocking sealed single-use items isn't an aerosol-generating activity.

B.q: Space is tight, so sterilised pouches are being stored on a shelf directly above the dirty sink. What is the main concern?
options: The pouches will dry out too quickly
The shelf will be harder to reach
Splashes may contaminate the packs
The sink will become blocked
B.why: Clean packs must be stored in a dedicated clean area, never above or below a dirty sink where splashes and aerosols can reach them.

whyNot.0: Drying isn't the issue; pouches should be dry anyway.
whyNot.1: Reach is a minor point; contamination is the real risk.
whyNot.3: Shelving above a sink doesn't block it; splash contamination is the concern.

C.q: Which sequence correctly shows how instruments move through the decontamination room?
options: Receive, sterilise, clean, inspect, store
Receive, inspect, sterilise, clean, store
Receive, clean, sterilise, inspect, store
Receive, clean, inspect, sterilise, store
C.why: Instruments are received dirty, cleaned, inspected (and packed), sterilised, then stored. Inspection must come after cleaning and before sterilising.

whyNot.0: Sterilising before cleaning bakes debris on and fails to sterilise.
whyNot.1: You can't usefully inspect for cleanliness before the instrument has been cleaned.
whyNot.2: Inspection after sterilisation is too late to catch soil that blocked the steam.

C.q: Agency staff are covering the decontamination room this week. Which measure would best help them keep to the workflow?
options: A list of the day's patients
Clear dirty and clean zone signs
A copy of the staff rota
Extra boxes of gloves on the bench
C.why: Clear labelling of dirty and clean zones helps new or temporary staff follow the one-way flow correctly.

whyNot.0: The patient list doesn't explain how the room works.
whyNot.2: The rota tells people when to work, not how to keep zones separate.
whyNot.3: Gloves help with PPE but don't show the direction of the workflow.

C.q: Two trays are mixed up during a busy list and you can't tell which is clean and which is dirty. What should you do?
options: Use the tidier-looking tray first
Ask the dentist which one they want
Treat both as dirty and reprocess them
Wipe both trays and put them away
C.why: If status is uncertain, treat items as dirty: stop, separate, and send them back through decontamination.

whyNot.0: Looking tidy doesn't prove an instrument has been sterilised.
whyNot.1: The dentist can't confirm processing status by looking either.
whyNot.3: Wiping is not sterilisation, so this risks using contaminated instruments.

reteach.title: Think of it like a kitchen
reteach.question: A good restaurant kitchen never lets raw chicken touch the plates going out to diners. How does the decontamination room do the same job?

blocks.h: Raw in one end, ready out the other
blocks.body: In a kitchen, raw food comes in at one end, is prepared and cooked, and plated food leaves from the other end. Nobody carries raw meat across the serving counter. The decontamination room works the same way: used instruments come in at the dirty end, are cleaned and inspected, sterilised, and leave from the clean end. If a dirty tray lands on the clean bench, it's like putting raw chicken on a serving plate: everything it touched has to be dealt with again.

blocks.text: The rule works in both directions: dirty never goes forward into the clean zone, and clean never goes backwards into the dirty zone (no clean packs near the dirty sink, no shared trolleys).

explain.body: Instruments move through receive, wash, rinse, inspect and pack, sterilise and store in a single direction. No stage may recontaminate an instrument via a surface used at an earlier stage.

test.q: Instruments have finished processing. Which item should move LAST in a correctly organised workflow?
options: Sterilised packs into storage
Used trays into the wash sink
Rinsed instruments to inspection
Inspected instruments into pouches
test.why: Sterilised packs going into clean storage is the final step of the dirty-to-clean flow.

whyNot.1: Washing is near the start of the flow.
whyNot.2: Inspection happens before packing and sterilising.
whyNot.3: Packing comes before sterilisation and storage.

explain.body: The dirty receiving bench is used for nothing else and sits beside the washing stage. The sterilizer is well away from other activities, and clean storage is at the far end. Air should move from clean to dirty where possible.

test.q: In a well-designed decontamination room, which way should air move where possible?
options: From dirty areas to clean areas
From clean areas to dirty areas
Upwards from the sinks to the store
It doesn't matter in small rooms
test.why: HTM 01-05 says air movement should be from clean to dirty, so contaminated aerosols are carried away from processed instruments.

whyNot.0: Dirty-to-clean airflow would carry aerosols onto sterilised instruments.
whyNot.2: Aerosols from sinks should be carried away from storage, not towards it.
whyNot.3: Airflow matters in every decontamination area, whatever its size.

explain.body: Essential quality requirements are the minimum: a designated area, separated from clinical work by space or time. Best practice adds a separate decontamination room, a validated washer-disinfector and better storage.

test.q: A practice decontaminates instruments at a designated bench in the surgery. Which statement is correct under HTM 01-05?
options: It is not allowed under any circumstances
It meets best practice if the bench is long
It can meet essential quality requirements
It is acceptable only for wrapped instruments
test.why: A designated area in or next to the surgery, separated by space or time, can meet the essential quality requirements; practices should plan towards a separate room.

whyNot.0: HTM 01-05 explicitly allows this at the essential level.
whyNot.1: Best practice needs a separate decontamination room, not a longer bench.
whyNot.3: Wrapping has nothing to do with where decontamination takes place.

explain.body: Change gloves and perform hand hygiene between dirty and clean tasks. Never share trolleys, carry dirty items through clean areas, or put notes and pens on the dirty bench. If things get mixed up: stop, separate, clean the surface, reprocess anything uncertain.

rows.label: One trolley for clean and dirty loads
Fresh gloves before handling clean packs
Logbook resting on the dirty bench

test.q: A nurse finishes scrubbing instruments and reaches for the sealed pouches without changing gloves. What principle has been broken?
options: Stock rotation
Zone separation
Parametric release
Pressure safety
test.why: Gloves used for dirty work carry contamination; they must be removed, with hand hygiene, before handling clean items.

whyNot.0: Stock rotation is about using older packs first.
whyNot.2: Parametric release is about checking cycle data before releasing a load.
whyNot.3: Pressure safety relates to the sterilizer as a pressure vessel.
